title: Distance Totals From Every Node
statement:
An undirected tree has n nodes labelled 0 to n − 1 and is given as a list of n − 1 edges, where edges[i] = [u, v] connects u and v. Every edge has length 1.

For each node i, add up its distances to all other nodes. Return an array totals of length n where totals[i] is that sum.

examples.why: From node 2: one step to 0, 3 and 4, two steps to 1, so 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5. Node 1 is the farthest out: 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9.
A single node has no one to be far from.
The middle node is 1 away from both ends; each end is 1 + 2 = 3 from the others.

constraints: The edges form a tree; it can be a long path
hints: One BFS gives the total for one node in O(n). Doing it for every node is O(n²). How does the total change when you move from a node to its neighbour?
Root the tree at 0. Moving the start from a parent p to its child c brings every node in c's subtree one step closer and every other node one step farther.
So totals[c] = totals[p] − size[c] + (n − size[c]). Compute subtree sizes and totals[0] in one pass, then push the totals downward in a second pass.

explain.intuition:
Computing each total from scratch repeats almost all the work. Compare two neighbours instead. Root the tree at 0 and look at an edge from parent p to child c. If you stand at c instead of p, the size[c] nodes in c's subtree each get one step closer, and the other n − size[c] nodes each get one step farther. Nothing else changes.

So the totals follow from each other: totals[c] = totals[p] + n − 2 · size[c]. One pass from the bottom computes every subtree size and the total for the root (the sum of all depths). A second pass from the top fills in everyone else. This "rerooting" trick turns n separate searches into two passes.
steps: Build an adjacency list. Get a BFS (or iterative DFS) order from node 0 and each node's parent and depth.
totals[0] is the sum of all depths.
Walk the order backwards to compute subtree sizes: size[v] = 1 + sum of its children's sizes.
Walk the order forwards: for every non-root v, set totals[v] = totals[parent[v]] + n − 2 · size[v].
pitfalls: Running a BFS from every node: correct, but 30 000² steps is far too slow.
Writing both passes as plain recursion. A tree that is one long path makes the recursion 30 000 levels deep and overflows the stack, especially in Python.
Mixing up the direction of the update: the child's own subtree gets closer, so subtract size[c], and add the rest.

solutions.title: BFS from every node
solutions.idea: Run a BFS from each node and add up the distances.

solutions.title: Rerooting with two passes
solutions.idea: Sizes and the root's total bottom-up, then totals[c] = totals[p] + n − 2·size[c] top-down. Iterative, so a long path is safe.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def distanceTotals(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for u, v in edges:
            adj[u].append(v)
            adj[v].append(u)
        parent, depth = [-1] * n, [0] * n
        seen = [False] * n
        seen[0] = True
        order = [0]
        for u in order:  # BFS order; the list grows while we walk it
            for v in adj[u]:
                if not seen[v]:
                    seen[v] = True
                    parent[v], depth[v] = u, depth[u] + 1
                    order.append(v)
        size = [1] * n
        for v in reversed(order[1:]):
            size[parent[v]] += size[v]
        totals = [0] * n
        totals[0] = sum(depth)
        for v in order[1:]:
            totals[v] = totals[parent[v]] + n - 2 * size[v]
        return totals

followups: Edges now have different positive lengths. How does the rerooting formula change?
Return the node with the smallest total (a centre of the tree). Can you find it without computing every total?
